claim: UNICEF and ITU estimate 1.3 billion school-age children lack home internet access and two-thirds of schools in low-income countries lack any internet connection, with the divide concentrated in Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia.

source.title: How many children and young people have internet access at home?

method: Reviewed UNICEF/ITU report methodology, household survey compilation, and school-level connectivity estimates.
limitations: The 1.3 billion figure is from 2020 — connectivity may have improved since then in some countries but the direction and magnitude of change is not systematically tracked.
School connectivity estimates are modeled from available surveys and may miss recent infrastructure investments.
Home access varies substantially within countries — national averages mask enormous sub-national and wealth-tercile gaps.
The 'two-thirds of schools' figure is a low-income-country aggregate — individual countries range from near-zero to over 50 percent connected.

claim: Giga, a UNICEF-ITU initiative, has mapped school locations and connectivity status for over 1 million schools across 30 countries using satellite imagery and ML, providing the most comprehensive school-connectivity dataset available.

source.title: Giga: Connect every school to the Internet

method: Reviewed Giga methodology documentation, school-mapping approach, connectivity-classification algorithm, and country-coverage assessment.
limitations: Satellite-based connectivity classification may misclassify intermittent or mobile-only connectivity — a school with sporadic mobile coverage may be classified differently than one with reliable broadband.
Giga coverage is concentrated in partner countries — schools in non-partner countries are not mapped.
Connectivity classification is a snapshot — it does not capture whether connectivity is actually used for educational purposes.
The ML-based school-location detection has false-positive and false-negative rates that vary by geography and building type.

claim: UNESCO UIS SDG 4.a.1 metadata keeps electricity, internet for pedagogical purposes, and computers for pedagogical purposes as separate school-service indicators, so a school-connectivity inventory must not treat an internet flag as a complete digital-learning-readiness measure.

source.title: SDG 4 Ensure inclusive and equitable quality education and promote lifelong learning opportunities for all — Metadata: 4.a.1 Proportion of schools offering basic services, by type of service

method: Reviewed the metadata definition, the separate concepts for electricity, internet for pedagogical purposes, and computers for pedagogical purposes, and the sample school-questionnaire items used for SDG 4.a.1.
limitations: The metadata defines indicators and questionnaire concepts; it does not provide current school-level observations for a target country.
The indicator does not establish bandwidth, uptime, latency, or whether pupils actually use the connection for learning.
It does not validate the completeness, currency, or independent ground truth of any national school census.
Cross-validation against Giga or performance measurements remains a country-specific task, not a property of this metadata document.

claim: The ITU DataHub provides internationally harmonized household and individual ICT indicators for about 200 economies, collected from national authorities and household ICT surveys; it is suitable for national connectivity context but not for locating unconnected schools.
method: Reviewed the ITU DataHub scope, collection process, harmonization statement, geographic coverage, and listed household-versus-school indicator grain.
limitations: The page describes household and individual ICT indicators rather than school-level observations.
Country-level indicators cannot identify which schools lack connectivity or distinguish school internet from household access.
The page does not provide a single observation date for every indicator; each downloaded series must retain its own year and metadata.
ITU distributes the data without a warranty and places interpretation responsibility on the user.

claim: The GSMA Mobile Connectivity Index methodology describes a country-level composite framework for mobile-network coverage, affordability, consumer readiness, and relevant content/services; it can contextualize school-connectivity analysis but cannot replace school-level measurement.
method: Reviewed the methodology report's unit of analysis, component domains, indicator construction, and stated interpretation limits before classifying it as a contextual source.
limitations: The index is country-level and composite; it does not identify school locations or school-specific service quality.
A national mobile-connectivity score does not establish that a school has reliable electricity, a usable connection, devices, or educational content.
Index components and weights create interpretation risk if treated as a direct outcome measure.
The methodology report does not provide independent ground truth for each school's connectivity status.

claim: The UNESCO Institute for Statistics guide recommends collecting ICT-in-education indicators through official education records and defines a measurement framework that can improve comparability of school connectivity data, but it is methodological guidance rather than a current sub-national dataset.

source.title: Guide to Measuring Information and Communication Technologies (ICT) in Education

method: Reviewed the guide's recommended administrative-data collection setting, indicator definitions, proposed questionnaire items, and distinction between measurement guidance and observed country data.
limitations: The guide was published in 2011; it is a historical measurement standard and may not reflect later platform, device, or connectivity changes.
The guide does not supply current school-level observations for a target country.
Following a measurement standard does not establish that a national school census is complete, current, or independently validated.
Cross-country comparability still depends on implementation, response completeness, and metadata from each education system.
The guide cannot measure bandwidth, reliability, or actual educational use by itself.

claim: Giga's mapping service combines official school and connectivity data from government partners with open data, uses satellite imagery, machine learning, and open-source mapping tools for data refinement, and exposes API access to school location, connectivity status, and internet-quality layers; it is therefore a multi-source compilation rather than a single ground-truth measurement.

source.title: How we work | Mapping School Connectivity | Giga

method: Reviewed the mapping page sections on source integration, API downloads, data-quality assessment, satellite and machine-learning refinement, and local validation campaigns; recorded the page's year only because it does not expose an exact publication or update date.
limitations: The page does not expose an exact publication or update date; 2025-01-01 is a year-level source-date proxy and must not be read as a precise release date.
Government, open-map, and other partner layers can have different definitions, update cycles, and missingness; the API does not make them homogeneous ground truth.
The page does not provide country-specific sensitivity, specificity, sampling-frame, or independent validation estimates for every connectivity classification.
School-location refinement and connectivity status do not establish bandwidth, uptime, electricity reliability, device access, or educational use.

claim: Giga Meter describes school-level end-user performance monitoring through up to four automated daily tests of download speed, upload speed, latency, and uptime, with ISP network-edge data as a complementary vantage point; it can supply a quality layer beyond a connected/not-connected flag but cannot measure pedagogical use.

source.title: Monitoring School Connectivity | Giga Meter | Giga

method: Reviewed the monitoring documentation's stated test cadence, measured performance fields, data access path, ISP integration, and multi-vantage-point cross-referencing language; recorded the year only because the page does not expose an exact publication or update date.
limitations: The page does not expose an exact publication or update date; 2026-01-01 is a year-level catalog date for the current page, not a dated measurement release.
The documentation does not establish country-wide school coverage, a representative sample, or completeness of the participating-school panel.
Up to four tests per day may not represent all-day reliability, peak congestion, outages outside the test windows, or service experienced on other devices.
Performance tests do not observe electricity continuity, device availability, teacher capability, relevant content, or actual educational use.

claim: UNESCO UIS World Education Statistics 2024 reports that the latest available SDG 4.a.1 school-facility data are from 2023 while noting that the 2022 sample is more representative, demonstrating why school-connectivity analyses must retain both observation year and representativeness metadata.
method: Reviewed the school-facilities section covering SDG 4.a.1 and recorded the document's explicit distinction between the latest 2023 data and the more representative 2022 sample; treated the URL path as month-level publication evidence.
limitations: The report presents global and regional aggregates, not a school-level or district-level connectivity map.
The latest year and the more representative sample are not necessarily the same observation frame; they must not be silently combined.
The report does not cross-validate national administrative records against Giga or repeated performance measurements.
School internet availability is not equivalent to bandwidth, uptime, electricity reliability, device access, or actual learning use.

claim: The pinned Giga Maps backend data-source configuration separates a boolean connectivity field and connectivity type from school-level quality-of-service fields for download speed, upload speed, and latency, while marking the configuration draft; it is useful for provenance and schema inspection, not for validating observed coverage.

source.title: Giga Maps backend data source configuration (data_sources.json)

method: Reviewed the pinned configuration entries for the Daily Check App and QoS sources, including field names, units, access requirements, and the explicit DRAFT status; used the commit-pinned URL to prevent branch drift.
limitations: This is a source configuration file, not an observation dataset and not evidence of country coverage or school-level prevalence.
The pinned configuration marks the listed sources as DRAFT, so field definitions require confirmation against the live API before extraction.
The file does not provide ground-truth accuracy, missingness rates, or cross-validation results against school census data.
The configuration is historical as of 2024-07-16; current APIs or schemas may have changed.
